podcast.title: Blackwork Warrior Tattoo
podcast.body: Tim Commerford is known for what is described as potentially the "biggest, most dense tattoo in the history of rock." It is a Blackwork tattoo, characterized by a warrior-like pattern that extensively covers his biceps, pecs, shoulders, and extends across his entire back down to spirals on his cheeks, appearing almost as one solid piece of clothing. "It's a warrior-like pattern that covers his biceps, pecs, and shoulders. And it also extends across his entire back all the way down to some spirals on his cheeks. It's almost one solid piece. It looks like he's wearing a piece of clothing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Life and Family
podcast.body: Timmy Comerford's father was a rocket scientist, specifically an engineer who worked on the space shuttle, while his mother was a mathematician and a teacher. His family life was troubled, marked by his mother's brain cancer diagnosis which led her to move away, a subsequent divorce, a stepmother, and the death of his biological mother in 1988. "His dad was a rocket scientist. Now seriously, a rocket scientist."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Implosion (October 18, 2000) – Zack de la Rocha's Departure
xref.body: Rage Against the Machine experienced an "implosion" on October 18, 2000, when their singer, Zack de la Rocha, quit the band. Despite this, the remaining three members—Tom Morello, Tim Commerford, and Brad Wilk—decided to stay together and search for a new vocalist, leading to the formation of Audioslave. "Singer and Zacti La Roca quit the band on October 18, 2000, and frankly, that was fine as far as the other three guys were concerned. They planned to stay together."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Band Formation and Political Stance
xref.body: Rage Against the Machine formed after finding members through musicians-wanted classified ads. Over eight years, they earned a reputation as one of the most political and funkiest bands in the alternative nation, largely due to the contributions of Tim Commerford and Brad Wilk. "Over the next eight years rage against the machine got a rep as one of the most political bands in the alternative nation and one of the funkiest thanks to Tim Bob and Brad Wilk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Formation from Rage Against the Machine Remnants – Producer's Suggestion
xref.body: Audioslave formed when the remaining members of Rage Against the Machine (Tom Morello, Tim Commerford, Brad Wilk) sought a new singer after Zack de la Rocha's departure. Producer Rick Rubin suggested Chris Cornell, leading to an instant creative connection and the rapid composition of 21 songs. "Rage Against the Machine had imploded... All they needed to do was find a new singer... Then producer Rick Rubin suggested that they ring up Chris Cornell."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Powerful Bottom End
xref.body: A key element contributing to Rage Against the Machine's distinct sound was their powerful "bottom end," driven by bassist Tim Commerford and drummer Brad Wilk. Singer Zack de la Rocha and guitarist Tom Morello recognized the need to allow the rhythm section ample space to contribute to the band's overall sound. "One of the things that made Rage Against the Machine so cool was that bottom end."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Rage Against the Machine with Chris Cornell
xref.body: Audioslave was essentially the remaining members of Rage Against the Machine (Tom Morello, Tim Commerford, Brad Wilk) with Chris Cornell as the new frontman, resulting in a significant musical "makeover" from their original sound. "Audio Slave, which, let's be honest, is really Rage Against the Machine with a big Chris Cornell makeover."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Tim Commerford's Background and Influences
xref.body: Tim Commerford, known by various names including Tim Bob and Tim C, grew up in Irvine, south of Los Angeles. His mother was a mathematician and his father an aeronautical engineer who worked on the space shuttle. He and Zack de la Rocha formed their first band, Juvenile Expression, in grade seven, after Zack taught Tim to play bass using the Sex Pistols' "Never Mind the Bollocks" album. Tim also spent hours learning Geddy Lee's bass parts from Rush albums. "Mom was a mathematician while his dad was an aeronautical engineer who actually worked on the space shuttle."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
